author: lightclient
content: what is the reason it is hard to sweep accounts today? you don't know the exact price you'll be paying for gas? with 8141 is this solved since you can introspect from the smart account about the current gas price and available funds?

author: sky.cactus
content: The problem today is that at transaction construction time, you do not know how much gas will cost when your transaction is mined so you cannot set the `amount` field precisely.

author: lightclient

author: sky.cactus
content: I haven't been following 8141, so I'm not sure if it will solve this problem cleanly or not.  Will it allow sweeping with a single transaction and no overpayment?  Is there additional user friction (e.g., a signature as well as the transaction, needing a second account to pay for gas, etc.)?

author: donnoh

author: lightclient
content: i think the 8141-style solution here would be an opcode SWEEP, which would be a special type of APPROVE that takes a destination address and sends all eth value of the approving account to _and_ sets the address for any gas overrage refunds to be that destination address

author: sky.cactus
content: Does that align with how execution clients do gas accounting?

author: sky.cactus
content: Do they first deduct gas, and then at the end of the transaction "refund" it, and it isn't too big of a change to redirect this refund (or perhaps already a planned change)?

author: lightclient
content: yeah we deduct the full gas limit at the beginning of tx. in 8141 there is a "payer" actor, so in the case of SWEEP we can just set payer to be the sweep account after the full account value is deducted from the real payer

author: lightclient
content: or we keep the "payer" account the same and add a "sweep" account which when set, receives the refund. that's probably a bit better since we can retain the real payer in the tx receipt

author: lightclient
content: either way, seems pretty simple

author: lightclient
content: what i'm thinking is suppose you want to sweep A -> B. first SWEEP would execute the APPROVE semantics, which deduct the gas payment from A. then it would sweep remaining funds in A to the destination account B and set "payer" or "sweep" to B. at the end of tx execution, remaining any overage would go to B

author: lightclient
content: so technically B is not the payer, which is why the "sweep" context variable is probably a better choice

author: lightclient
